Minimum Risk Point Estimation of the Coefficient of Variation

Source: vignettes/mrpe-cv.Rmd
mrpe-cv.Rmd

The Research Question

The coefficient of variation, κ = σ / μ, expresses the standard deviation of a quantity relative to its mean, so it summarizes dispersion on a unit free scale. It is used wherever relative, rather than absolute, variability is the quantity of interest: the relative variability of assay measurements in the laboratory, of claim sizes in insurance, of response times in an experiment, or of household expenditures in survey research.

How many observations should be collected to estimate κ well? When each observation carries a cost (a record to audit, a participant to run, a sample to assay), collecting more data buys a more accurate estimate and spends more of the study budget. Minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) makes that trade explicit. Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) develop a purely sequential procedure that estimates κ while minimizing a risk that combines estimation error and sampling cost. Because the asymptotic variance of the sample coefficient of variation depends on the unknown population (through its third and fourth moments), the sample size cannot be fixed in advance; the data collected so far say whether to stop.

The Method

Write kn for the sample coefficient of variation after n observations, the sample standard deviation divided by the sample mean. The risk combines the expected squared estimation error, priced by a constant A, with the cost c of each observation (Equation 11 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2016):

Rn(κ) = A E[(kn − κ)2] + c n

For samples that are not too small the mean squared error is approximately ξ2 / n, where ξ2 is the asymptotic variance of √n (kn − κ), so the risk is approximately A ξ2 / n + c n (their Equation 14). That is smallest at the optimal fixed sample size (their Equation 15)

nc = (A / c)1/2 ξ

where it equals 2 c nc (their Equation 16). Because ξ2 is unknown, the purely sequential rule estimates it from the data after each observation; write Vn2 for the estimate from the first n. To keep a low early estimate from stopping the procedure too soon, a small correction term is added, and sampling stops at the first n at or beyond the pilot sample size with (their Equation 23)

n2 ≥ (A / c) (Vn2 + n−2γ)

where γ is a constant strictly between 0 and 1/2 (the article suggests 0.49, the default of the argument gamma). The pilot sample size is the larger of a minimum m0 and (A / c)1/(2 + 2γ), rounded up (their Equation 24, a form the article gives as following Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009).

The Sequential Workflow

seq_mr_cv_pilot() returns the pilot sample size, which depends only on the two cost constants, and seq_mr_cv() evaluates the stopping rule on the data collected so far and records the decision as an attribute. Neither collects data or keeps state: the analyst calls seq_mr_cv() again after each new observation. There is no confidence level, because the procedure targets a risk and not a confidence interval.

Suppose an actuary is estimating the relative variability of individual claim amounts (in thousands of dollars), which are positive and heavily right skewed. Auditing one claim costs one unit, and a unit of squared estimation error is priced at A = 900.

A <- 900      # price of one unit of squared estimation error
cost <- 1     # cost of auditing one claim record
pilot_n <- seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = A, c = cost)
pilot_n
#> [1] 10

To have data to work with, 100 claims are simulated here from a right skewed gamma distribution whose coefficient of variation is 1.29; they stand for the claims in the order they would be audited. The actuary audits the pilot sample and evaluates the rule.

set.seed(113)
claims <- rgamma(100, shape = 0.6, scale = 2)
check <- seq_mr_cv(claims[1:pilot_n], A = A, c = cost)
check
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 10
#>   Criterion n     : 24
#> 
#>   cv                : 1.378934
#>   risk              : 54.47553
#>   xi_squared        : 0.4941725
#>   optimal_n         : 24
#>   current_n         : 10
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

The criterion sample size implied by the pilot data exceeds the pilot sample size, so the rule is not met and auditing continues, one claim at a time, with a new check after each. In a study that is a call to seq_mr_cv() after each claim. With the claims already in hand, seq_path() makes the same sequence of checks in one call, and its plot shows the criterion moving as the claims arrive.

path <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, claims, A = A, c = cost)
attr(path, "stop_n")
#> [1] 36
plot(path, which = "criterion")

attr(path, "final_check")
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 36
#>   Criterion n     : 35
#> 
#>   cv                : 1.237414
#>   risk              : 67.75349
#>   xi_squared        : 1.27014
#>   optimal_n         : 35
#>   current_n         : 36
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE

The rule was first met at 36 claims, and that is where the audit ends: the estimate a sequential design reports is the one at the stopping point, not one from a later, more favorable sample size. The reported cv is the minimum risk point estimate of κ, and risk is the estimated risk there. MRPE returns a point estimate and no confidence interval, and the estimate carries the sampling error of a statistic computed at a modest sample size. seq_report() words the result for a methods section:

seq_report(path)
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential minimum risk point
#> estimation procedure for the coefficient of variation (Chattopadhyay &
#> Kelley, 2016), with a loss constant of A = 900 and a sampling cost of c
#> = 1 per observation. The stopping rule was evaluated from the pilot
#> sample size (n = 10) onward, after each additional observation, and was
#> first met at n = 36. At that sample size the estimate of the
#> coefficient of variation was 1.237.
#> 
#> Reference
#> Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient
#>     of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing
#>     sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research,
#>     51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Two situations are reported as “not met” whatever the sample size. If the variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (every observation so far is the same, or the sample gives a negative estimate), no variance has been estimated: the rule is reported as not met, the result carries attr(check, "variance_unusable") equal to TRUE, and a note is printed (see “An Unusable Variance Estimate” in help("SMSD-package")). Read literally, the article’s rule would stop at once on such an estimate; the package departs from it on purpose. A positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe (bounded below by n−3), so a small coefficient of variation, or a change in the units of the data, does not by itself make the estimate unusable. If the sample mean is zero or negative (or differs from zero only by rounding error, as for centered or standardized scores), the coefficient of variation cannot be estimated, and the result says so.

The first of these departures costs little when a negative estimate is rare, as it is for normal data: with a coefficient of variation of 0.10, A = 400, and c = 1 (a pilot sample size of 8), the mean final sample size in 2,000 simulated runs was 8.05, where the rule as printed gave 8.00. It can cost a great deal for a quantity that takes only two or three distinct values and has a small coefficient of variation, because the estimate is then negative at many stages in a row. With observations equal to 9 or 11 with equal probability and the same constants, the rule as printed stopped at 8 in every run; seq_mr_cv() stopped at 8 in about half of the runs and kept sampling in the rest, to a mean final sample size of 25, a 99th percentile of 244, and a largest value of 693. For a quantity of that kind, decide on a largest sample size before sampling begins. (These figures are from the simulations reported in ?seq_mr_cv.)

Two Variance Estimators

The argument variance of seq_mr_cv() selects the estimator Vn2.

The default, variance = "corrected", is the estimator of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equations 31 and 32), the sample version of the asymptotic variance of the coefficient of variation for a general population (their Equation 30),

ξ2 = μ4 / (4 μ2 σ2) − σ2 / (4 μ2) − μ3 / μ3 + σ4 / μ4

where μ3 and μ4 are the third and fourth central moments. It is the estimator that seq_aipe_cv() uses.

The alternative, variance = "published", is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016), the sample version of their Equation 9,

μ4 / (4 μ4) + σ4 / (4 μ4) − μ3 / μ3 + σ2 / (2 μ2)

The first expression minus the second is κ2 (1 − κ2) / 4 times the excess kurtosis, μ4 / σ4 − 3. The two are therefore the same for a normal population, and for any population with no excess kurtosis, and they differ otherwise. For a population with heavier tails than the normal and κ below 1 the published expression is the smaller of the two, so the procedure stops before the sample size that minimizes the risk. For a gamma population with κ = 0.8:

shape <- 1 / 0.8^2                    # gamma, unit scale: kappa = 0.8
mu <- shape
sigma2 <- shape
mu3 <- 2 * shape                      # third central moment
mu4 <- 3 * shape * (shape + 2)        # fourth central moment
xi2 <- c(
  corrected = mu4 / (4 * mu^2 * sigma2) - sigma2 / (4 * mu^2) -
    mu3 / mu^3 + sigma2^2 / mu^4,
  published = mu4 / (4 * mu^4) + sigma2^2 / (4 * mu^4) -
    mu3 / mu^3 + sigma2 / (2 * mu^2)
)
xi2
#> corrected published 
#>  0.524800  0.303616
kappa2 <- sigma2 / mu^2               # the difference, and the identity
c(difference = xi2[["corrected"]] - xi2[["published"]],
  identity = kappa2 * (1 - kappa2) / 4 * (mu4 / sigma2^2 - 3))
#> difference   identity 
#>   0.221184   0.221184
sqrt(5000000 / 10 * xi2)              # the sample size each one aims at
#> corrected published 
#>  512.2499  389.6255

Simulation shows which expression describes the estimator. In 200,000 samples of 400 observations from that population, n times the mean squared error of kn was 0.516 (standard error 0.002), beside the 0.525 and 0.304 just computed. In the full procedure with A = 5,000,000 and c = 10, for which the risk is smallest at 512 observations, the mean final sample size in 5,000 replications was 479 with the corrected estimator and about 374 with the published one. (Both simulations are reported in the Details of ?seq_mr_cv.) Table 1 of the article (p. 642) reports 374.0 for this population, beside an optimal sample size of 390, which is the value the published expression gives.

Use the default. The published estimator is offered so that the article’s worked example and tables, and the results of mr_cv() in DMAR and mr.cv() in MBESS (which use the published form), can be reproduced. The derivation of both expressions by the delta method, with the algebra written out and a simulation a reader can run, is in a note installed with the package:

file.exists(system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD"))
#> [1] TRUE

Reproducing the Published Example

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, pp. 637 to 638) estimate the coefficient of variation of the number of age appropriate books in the homes of third graders. A home visit costs 75 dollars, and the team would pay 1,000 dollars to estimate κ to within 0.05, so A = 1,000 / 0.052 = 400,000. The pilot sample size is 18.

seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = 400000, c = 75)
#> [1] 18

With the article’s own variance, the 18 pilot observations give the risk and estimate printed in the article (5964.345 and 0.7391157), and the rule is not met.

books <- c(36, 53, 19, 11, 10, 24, 14, 65, 18, 48, 25, 35, 13, 18, 3, 41,
           5, 3, 44, 26, 13, 39, 2, 3, 26, 22, 8, 15, 12, 22, 5, 21, 23,
           40, 18)
seq_mr_cv(books[1:18], A = 400000, c = 75, variance = "published")
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 18
#>   Criterion n     : 38
#> 
#>   cv                : 0.7391157
#>   risk              : 5964.345
#>   xi_squared        : 0.2076455
#>   optimal_n         : 38
#>   current_n         : 18
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
#> 
#>   Note: The variance estimate is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and
#>         Kelley (2016), as requested with variance = "published". It
#>         agrees with the default estimator for normal data and can
#>         differ otherwise; see ?seq_mr_cv.

The article adds observations one at a time, and the rule is met for the first time at the 35th, with risk 4891.284.

published <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, books, A = 400000, c = 75,
                      variance = "published")
attr(published, "stop_n")
#> [1] 35
attr(published, "final_check")
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 35
#>   Criterion n     : 35
#> 
#>   cv                : 0.7013904
#>   risk              : 4891.284
#>   xi_squared        : 0.1982998
#>   optimal_n         : 35
#>   current_n         : 35
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
#> 
#>   Note: The variance estimate is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and
#>         Kelley (2016), as requested with variance = "published". It
#>         agrees with the default estimator for normal data and can
#>         differ otherwise; see ?seq_mr_cv.

With the default variance the same 35 observations never meet the rule (stop_n is NA); the criterion at the 35th asks for one more.

corrected <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, books, A = 400000, c = 75)
attr(corrected, "stop_n")
#> [1] NA
attr(corrected, "final_check")
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 35
#>   Criterion n     : 36
#> 
#>   cv                : 0.7013904
#>   risk              : 4977.259
#>   xi_squared        : 0.2058226
#>   optimal_n         : 36
#>   current_n         : 35
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

What to Expect Before the Study

seq_mr_cv_sensitivity() runs the whole procedure many times on simulated data with a known coefficient of variation and compares the result with the best fixed sample size. For the actuary’s problem, with gamma claims whose coefficient of variation is 1.3:

sens <- seq_mr_cv_sensitivity(true_value = 1.3, A = A, c = cost,
                              distribution = "gamma", G = 500, seed = 2016)
sens
#> term                value
#> true_value          1.3
#> loss_A              900
#> cost                1
#> replications        500
#> optimal_n           45.22991
#> minimum_risk        90.45983
#> mean_n              26.48
#> median_n            25
#> sd_n                8.214167
#> ratio_n             0.5854533
#> mean_estimate       1.215112
#> mean_risk           83.28198
#> risk_efficiency     0.9206516
#> se_risk_efficiency  0.03771794
#> regret              -7.177841
#> pct_hit_max_n       0

optimal_n is the fixed sample size that minimizes the large sample risk for this population, and minimum_risk is the risk there. ratio_n compares the mean final sample size with the optimum, and risk_efficiency compares the mean realized loss with the minimum risk; it should be read against its Monte Carlo standard error, se_risk_efficiency.

The result is a caution about small studies of heavily skewed quantities. With A = 900 the procedure takes about 26 claims on average, where the best fixed sample size is 45. The variance estimate rests on the third and fourth sample moments, which are very variable in small samples from a population this skewed, and sampling ends the first time the criterion is met, so a low estimate ends it early. The guarantees of the procedure are asymptotic: the ratio approaches 1 as A / c grows, but slowly here. In the runs reported in the Details of ?seq_mr_cv, for the same population and cost, the ratio was about 0.58, 0.74, 0.85, and 0.93 with A equal to 900, 9,000, 90,000, and 900,000. The benchmark is itself a large sample approximation, which is why the risk efficiency can fall below 1 at sample sizes this small; that does not mean the procedure did better than the best fixed design. For a milder population the agreement is closer: in the same Details, with A = 5,000,000 and c = 10 (5,000 replications), the ratio was about 0.99 for gamma data with κ = 0.4, and the ratio of the realized risk to the minimum risk was within about 0.03 of 1.

Running the same call with variance = "published", distribution = "lognormal", or a batch size (batch, the number of observations added between checks) shows how each choice changes the picture.

Relationship to Accuracy in Parameter Estimation

SMSD supports the coefficient of variation in two ways. Use seq_mr_cv() when the design goal is to minimize a loss that balances accuracy against the cost of sampling. Use seq_aipe_cv() when the goal is a confidence interval of a target width, that is, accuracy in parameter estimation through a narrow interval (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018; Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008). With the default variance the two procedures share one distribution free estimator of the asymptotic variance and answer different design questions.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535
